newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces heart surgery, future unclear.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces heart surgery, future unclear.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin has ended months of silence and rumours about the state of his health by announcing to Russians that he would undergo heart surgery, probably later this month.

He gave no details in an interview broadcast by all the main television networks on Thursday about the nature of the operation, leaving the world guessing about the chances that he would be able to serve out his four-year second term.
His broadcast prompted immmediate speculation about a succession battle. Some political analysts predicted that his chief of staff, Anatoly Chubais, would govern in his absence.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who would take power temporarily if Yeltsin were unable to rule, and security chief Alexander Lebed were also seen as possible rivals.
Yeltsin's main rival in the presidential election, communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, called for a meeting between parliamentary faction leaders.
Such a meeting could help avoid destabilisation of the situation, Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
Russian stock prices fell sharply on news of the operation and investors sold European currencies for dollars on fears that any political upset in Moscow would spill westward.

Yeltsin, 65, said: "I have undergone routine checks and during these checks they have found something wrong with my heart. Recommendations of doctors, our doctors, were for an operation or to work in a passive way."

He spoke slowly, but with some of the sparkle he displayed in his re-election campaign, in the broadcast which followed two months of defensive statements by aides that he was absent from public view merely because he was tired.
"Passive work has never suited me. Nor can it suit me now. That's why an operation and full recovery, as they promise, is better for me than passive activity, passive work," he said.
Yeltsin's broadcast came a step closer to dismantling the taboos surrounding the condition of Kremlin leaders. In Soviet days, nothing was revealed about the state of the leader's health.

When hardline communist leader Leonid Brezhnev was in his decline, the Kremlin falsified pictures and staged events to hide his ill health. In the months before his successor Yuri Andropov died, officials said merely that he had a cold.
The liberal newspaper Sevodnya called Yeltsin's frank but delayed disclosure "a fact unprecedented in our political history".
But Nezavisimaya Gazeta also reflected on the equivocation of recent months: "This state secret hasn't been a secret for almost anyone for a long time," wrote the daily.

Yeltsin said he would probably have the operation in late September in the Moscow Cardiological Centre. "I do not want to go anywhere abroad," he said. "Our cardiological centre in Moscow is capable of performing such heart operations."
Yeltsin, who dropped almost completely from public view after defeating Zyuganov on July 3 to win a second term as president, looked tanned but tired in the broadcast.
He suffered two mild heart attacks and is now said to be suffering from ischaemic heart condition, which affects the blood supply to the heart muscle.

A Kremlin source told Reuters he expected that Yeltsin would undergo routine bypass surgery, in which veins from the leg or chest replace clogged cardiac arteries to improve blood supply to the heart.
Dr John Walwark, a top heart surgeon and director of transplant surgery at Papworth Hospital in Cambridge, England, told Britain's BBC radio that the procedure was fairly routine.
"We do about 30,000 of those operations in the U.K. and for his age and general fitness he should really have a very low risk of dying from the operation -- maybe around two percent," Walwark said.
Russian surgeon Mikhail Alshibaya told Ekho Moskvy radio restoring the heart's blood supply was a complicated procedure which had an average death rate of three to four percent.
"You can count the surgeons who do such operations in Russia on your fingers," he said. But he added that they did "a huge number" of them with basically the same results as in the West.
